en: The *Fuxing* (Subsidiary Commentary) fully contains the long passages and extensive meanings of the topical outlines (*kejie*) for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Among these, there are several sections and subsections where the intended meaning differs;

or where the meaning is the same yet difficult to discern from the text; or where the structural flow of the sections and subsections is inconsistent, being either expansive or concise. [I shall] briefly extract [these points].

I have prepared this outline and the enumeration of the sections and meanings for my own use, lest I forget; how could it be intended to show them to others? The explanation of the title has three parts:
first, the intent; second, the meaning; third, the textual intent. Regarding the textual intent, the Great Master himself said: "I shall explain the Dharma-gate realized within my own mind.

What is that which was realized? It is the Heart-Seal of all Buddhas. When was this realized? It was realized at Vulture Peak. Upon what scriptural authority is this based? [The text continues: "Distinct..."
The tradition relates that when the Great Master met Nanyue, Nanyue smiled and said, "In the past, we listened to the Lotus Sūtra together at Vulture Peak.

Chased by our past affinities, you have come here once more. The Great Master did not yet understand this. Nanyue said, "As an incarnate Bodhisattva, you have forgotten [your realization] through the course of rebirths.
You should enter the Samantabhadra practice hall. On the fourteenth day, his concentration and wisdom suddenly blossomed; from within that samādhi...
He rose and informed his teacher. The teacher said, "It is not that you have failed to realize it; it is not that I do not know. That which you have realized is the Lotus Samādhi.
As for the attainment of dhāraṇīs, you have attained the *Vartanī-dhāraṇī*.

From this day forward, among the thousands and tens of thousands of those who are textual Dharma masters or masters of dark realization through meditation, none shall be able to exhaustively fathom your eloquence. You shall be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma."

He was the most preeminent of his time. At the age of twenty-three, he attained the Seal of the Mind (cittamudrā). However, as the karmic conditions had not yet converged, there was no formal transmission of the lineage.

He merely lectured on such scriptures as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Yet, his profound understanding remained unexpressed. In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, at the age of fifty-seven, he returned to Jingzhou to repay the kindness of his birthplace.

He founded Yǔquán Monastery. Once the monastery was completed, he expounded on *zhìguān* (cessation and contemplation) to clarify the essential meaning of the [Lotus] Sūtra. This teaching did not differ from the various sūtras;
rather, it refined the mind to create the objective realm, deploying the ten vehicles (*shíchéng*) and the three thousand realms of existence (*sānqiān*) within a single thought-moment (*yīniàn*).

Transcending far beyond the limits of conventional doctrine, it stands preeminent and peerless. His intention was that those present in the assembly this day might immediately enter the Tathāgata’s chamber and don his robes.
Wearing the robe of the Tathāgata, sitting upon the seat of the Tathāgata, daily employing the Buddha-mind, and daily performing the Buddha-deeds.

As for the "Meaning," there are five layers of profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) originating from Tiantai. In explaining any sutra or śāstra, one must employ these five meanings; these five meanings encompass the entirety of a given work. They are:

Name (*nāman*), Substance (*vastu*), Principle (*abhiprāya*), Function (*kriyā*), and Teaching (*śāsana*). Regarding "Name": at the beginning of the scroll, it says "Samatha-vipaśyanā, luminous and tranquil," which is the explanation of the Name.

Furthermore, if one were to correlate these specifically with the text, they correspond to the "General Meaning" (*dà-yì*) within the five concise sections and the "Explanation of Names" (*shì-míng*) within the ten extensive sections.

The General Meaning is summarized in four aspects: teaching (*jiào*), discernment (*jiǎn*), truth (*dì*), and object (*jìng*). The Explanation of Names clarifies the contemplative wisdom (*guān-zhì*) through the relationship between the relative and the absolute. Since wisdom must illuminate an object, and when object and wisdom are in perfect accord, the name [of that wisdom] arises.
The General Meaning states: "Once one knows that ignorance is itself enlightenment, one no longer undergoes fluctuation. Thus it is said.

"Stilling" (*śamatha*) refers to the state of vast, luminous purity; "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to calling this state by that name. These two passages complete the explanation of the names. Second, the definition of the essence (*svabhāva*):

the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) is the essence. If we follow the text, it is found in the "Great Return" within the fivefold summary, and in the "Essence, Characteristics, and Final Goal" within the tenfold expansion.
These three sections all clarify the essence of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the three virtues. Although the *Zhǐguī* (Pointing to the Goal) does not explicitly state this, [it is implied].
The meaning is not different from the intent of the preceding two sections. Third, regarding the essence (*zong*): it is the essence of the mutual penetration of stillness and illumination.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "When concentration and wisdom are equal, one sees the Buddha-nature. The text states: "The two hands rub each other alternately; cloud and sun assist one another, only then bringing forth the tusks of the elephant.
According to the text, this refers to the "Great Practice" within the five summaries and the "Correct Cultivation" within the ten expansions; these are the two gates.
This is the sovereign lord of this single teaching; it is the ultimate destination for practitioners and the locus for cultivating the mind.

As for the function of the fourfold discernment: its function is to exhaustively dismantle [delusion] and realize perfection. Through exhaustive dismantling, there are no delusions that are not eliminated; through the realization of perfection, there are no virtues that are not fully possessed.

Within the five summaries, there is the realization of great fruits; within the ten expansions, there is the horizontal and vertical pervasion of destruction. The eighth is the retribution of fruit; these three passages are such. Regarding the characteristics of the five teachings:
first, the characteristics of the teachings are presented through the mutual interrelation of the many and the one. Within the five summaries, there is the tearing of the great net;

within the ten expansions, there are the four gates of the inclusion of phenomena, the partial and the perfect, and skillful means—all of which are characteristics of the teachings. Therefore, from within a single minute atom, [the teachings] emerge.
In this *Mahā-sāhasra-koṭi* scripture, the eight teachings and five flavors are all derived from the single mind; thus, the characteristics of the teachings are clear.

For the time being, let us divide the text according to its formal correspondence. However, according to the perfect (encompassing) intent, every single phrase and every single meaning contains all five [flavors].

This is "dividing without dividing" and "not dividing while dividing"—it must certainly be grasped through the mind. *Mahā* is a term of high praise. *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) refers to the realization...
This clarifies the nature of the mind. Initially, Zhiyan (Zhang’an) titled it *Yuántùn* (Perfect and Sudden); later, he changed it to *Móhē* (Mahā). What was his intention in making this change?

*Yuántùn* is a title denoting the most supreme; *Móhē* implies comprehensive inclusion. From the perspective of principle (*lǐ*), the supreme is appropriate; from the perspective of teaching (*jiào*), comprehensive inclusion is appropriate.

Comprehensive inclusion encompasses the threefold [teachings], thereby subsuming the gradual, the indeterminate, and all five periods and eight teachings. Therefore, he changed it accordingly. *Móhē*.
The three meanings of *ha* (great) are translated as "great," "many," and "superior. These three are all absolute; they do not receive their names in relation to the small, the few, or the inferior.

Phenomena (*dharma*) are neither small nor great, neither one nor many, neither superior nor inferior. This is because the small is itself the great, the one is itself the many, and the inferior is itself the superior.
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is perfectly wondrous and free from obstruction. Therefore, a single speck of dust and a single hair-tip encompass everything.

This is the inclusion of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Now, "Great" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "Many" refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*); and "Supreme" refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*).

These three are all fully present within a single form, a single fragrance, and a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). The quiescence of a single thought-moment, which perfectly encompasses the Dharma-realm, is *śamatha*;

the luminous clarity of a single thought-moment, which perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm, is *vipaśyanā*. *Śamatha* is *prajñā*, and *vipaśyanā* is *vimukti*. The non-duality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is—
The Dharma-body: in terms of the mind, it is called the three contemplations; in terms of objects, it is called the three truths; in terms of essence, it is called the three virtues;
in terms of function, it is called the three bodies; in terms of nature, it is called the three nirvāṇas; and in terms of wisdom, it is called the three enlightenments.

Among ordinary beings, these are called the Three Paths; among sages, they are called the Triple Gem. Although there are a thousand divergent ways regarding delusion and awakening, gain and loss, the single nature has never undergone change.
In previous generations, it was unheard of that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the mothers of the Buddhas of the three periods;

it was unheard of that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the ancestral masters of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; and it was unheard of that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constitute all teachings, principles, practices, and stages.

The Master [said]: "I have never heard that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* serve as the mirror of wisdom for all students. I have never heard that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* illuminate one's own body and mind such that they are entirely identical to the virtues of a Buddha;
this is because it causes one to rejoice in having personally heard [the teaching] at the feet of the Great Master.

The Confucian teaching speaks of innate knowledge (*shengzhi*) as the principle of a single lifetime. The Buddhist analysis distinguishes the three periods of time (*trikāla*) to establish the nature (*xing*). All phenomena (*dharmas*) have their ultimate origin in conditions (*pratyaya*), and thus arise."

Nature is eternally empty; it is called the True Principle of Heaven. This principle does not exist independently, but is ever-present within the myriad conditions (*pratyaya*). One who embraces both conditions and principle is called a Great Being (*mahāsattva*);

one who grasps at principle through deluded conditions is said to belong to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). By grasping at conditions through deluded principles, one wanders through the nine realms of existence.

To return to the root and revert to the source, one must rely on the transmission of a teacher. When the fundamental realm is illuminated, it is quiescent; I have no teacher or protector. As the Sūtra says: "One cannot attain [it] alone."
Because of the Dharma, one receives the prediction (vyākaraṇa). The prediction requires a teacher; it cannot exist without a teacher.

The teacher does not exclusively belong to the cause, for there is the contemplation of principle (li); yet there is no teacher who does not exclusively belong to the fruit, for the Buddha is the teacher and the Dharma is eternal.

If one claims that the Truth does not exist apart from the phenomena of causes and conditions—that ordinary beings have not yet realized it while the noble wisdom (āryajñāna) alone attests to it—this is the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna). It is precisely my contemplative wisdom that illuminates [it].
That all things arising through causes and conditions are devoid of self-nature and thus utterly non-existent is the Perfectly Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao).

In this Perfectly Sudden Teaching, one enters the stage of Buddhahood upon its manifestation; the myriad practices and myriad virtues are fully contained within a single thought-moment. The *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) in ten fascicles explains this a thousand times over.

If one does not believe this, the Tiantai school of teachings will perish. As for why the Deer Park did not speak of it while the Place of Enlightenment did, it was merely following the traces of the Buddha’s career.

It is said that following the ancestral lineage is convenient; however, if one considers the original teaching, what prevents all twenty-four patriarchs from having traversed the ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*?
Regarding the nine generations of patriarchs—such as Rong, Ji, Jue, Ji, Yi, and others—the refutation of these ancient claims appears in the subsequent text.

Since this is not the correct meaning, the status of these ancestors is not established. Therefore, the designation of "nine generations" should be deleted from here. Within the three [categories] of the total *anāsrava* (outflow-free), this...

The passage by Duan Wen presents difficulties for both ancient and modern scholars. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), spanning four pages, explains this while simultaneously refuting ancient interpretations.

Regarding the "nine points that cannot be lectured upon," the narrative is exceedingly prolix and chaotic. Yesterday, I examined the original text; the wording follows the preceding section closely: [one] stops fire, blood, and weapons to reach the three good realms; next, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);
next, one cultivates the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) path; next, one cultivates compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*); and finally, one cultivates the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is the text.
Furthermore, if the untainted (*anāsrava*) is taken as combined, there are only nine; if the untainted is expanded by dividing the two teachings and two vehicles into four, there are twelve.
The "four indeterminate" refers to the four within the essence, or it may point to the world below; the final "or" (*vā*) summarizes these four possibilities.

This refers to the meaning of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): because the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is difficult to understand, one relies on gradual and indeterminate guidance to advance the mind, whereby there are nine or ten propositions.
The three stages of the path lead one to eventually reach the true reality (*tathatā*); thus, there are these three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Generally speaking, there are four distinctions: gradual, indefinite, perfect, and sudden. First, regarding the classification by teaching (*yōu-chiao*):

among the eight teachings, there are the sudden, gradual, and indefinite. This refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, which is exclusively sudden; the five periods refer to the gradual arising of the gradual. Within each individual section, or...

Whether they are complete or incomplete is not fixed. Second, regarding the classification by *nikāya* (scriptural divisions): the *Avataṃsaka* is exclusively sudden; the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other *Āgamas* are exclusively gradual;
the *Vaipulya* is indeterminate; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is exclusively perfect. Third, regarding the classification by *dharma* (teachings):

as cited below from the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Anantārtha-nirdeśa*, and others, each possesses these three [aspects]. Fourth, regarding the meaning: all three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are the Great [Vehicle].
The vehicles all take the true reality (*dharmatā*) as their object; it is by borrowing the gradual and indeterminate [teachings] to assist the perfect cultivation that this is so.

The meanings of these four [gradual teachings] differ from one another; one should contemplate them deeply and avoid confusing them. Among these four gradual [teachings], the *Lotus Sūtra* possesses three types of gradualism.
The Great Master himself said: "From milk produced from a cow, up to clarified butter (*sarpis*). This is the proof of gradualism. This refers to the sequential order of the five periods.

"Birth" refers to gradualness, yet this is not a gradual dharma in the ordinary sense. Such a person should enter the Buddha’s wisdom through this dharma gradually; this describes how there was formerly such a gradual method.
Even raising a single hand or slightly bowing the head—this is the meaning of a person of the Perfect Teaching (the *yuan* [圓] vehicle) employing gradual methods as an aid to cultivation.

Regarding the divisions of the teachings, in the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) there is only the Perfect, with no further inclusion of the Separate (*bie* [別]), the Tripitaka (*san* [三]), or the Shared (*tong* [通]) vehicles. This is the assembly [of the teaching].

Because all provisional and limited teachings ultimately return to the One Vehicle, there is no contradiction in establishing three gradual stages according to time, dharma, and meaning; nor does this detract from the Perfection (the *yuan*). Sentient beings and the non-sentient are one.

As explained in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), Chapter Ten, "The Ten Stages of Understanding," the text and principles are exhaustive. Now, I shall assist with a further explanation: the distinction between the internal mind and external objects is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
To examine that the internal mind lacks intrinsic nature and external objects lack substantial reality is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, one contemplates through the principle.
In its essence, it has never been dual; in phenomena, it has never appeared as anything other than non-dual. This non-duality within duality is attained within a single thought-moment.

This wisdom that thoroughly realizes this single thought-moment is neither internal nor external, yet it is both internal and external. The ten directions and the three periods of time are contained solely within a single thought-moment;
outside of this thought, there is no phenomenon. This is the ultimate principle. If one were to claim that there is something within the thought or outside the thought...
The Dharma that can be apprehended is entirely illusory and not true wisdom. This true wisdom is designated as Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
When Buddha-nature manifests, how could there still exist the dualistic states of mind and object? Briefly, three gates are indicated; the main intent lies in the "sudden" (*tun*).
These three gates refer to the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* mentioned in the introduction: the gradual, the indeterminate, and the perfect-sudden. The main intent lies in the sudden.

It is exclusively *yuan* (perfect/round). According to the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the sequence of questions and answers regarding its arising was not the Great Master’s own analysis, but rather that of Zhizhe (Zhang’an).

The record states: "To simplify and abridge physical deportment is called 'one practice' (*yixing*); this does not refer to a single principle. Now, upon examining the intent of the sutra, it is from the perspective of principle that the name is derived.
The text says: "If one practices and studies as heard, one can enter the *yixing samādhi* and see all Buddhas face-to-face. Based on this, it is...
These four samādhis receive their names based on a single principle. Regarding sitting, walking, both walking and sitting, and neither walking nor sitting: these all proceed from a single practice.
The *Pratyutpanna*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Vaipulya* samādhis may be applied according to one’s inclination; they may all be contemplated from the perspective of principle.

Following the intent of the four types of samādhi, although the texts cited for śamatha and vipaśyanā differ, their essence is the same as that presented here; taking this intent as the standard, the general explanation is simply to penetrate the One.
Contemplate that one's own mind is the Dharma-realm. The Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings are identical in their non-abiding.
Fundamentally, the single Dharma-realm constitutes both body and land; there is neither "other" nor "self," neither root nor place of abiding, and neither cultivation nor non-cultivation.

There is neither realization nor non-realization; there are neither ordinary beings nor sages. It is only because sentient beings themselves claim to be bound by delusive thoughts that they consider themselves ordinary, unpracticed, or unrealized;

they consider the Buddha to be a sage, one who has realized and practiced the holy path, and one who has attained sainthood. These distinctions are established through the self-aggrandizement of sentient beings;
within the state of the Buddhas, none of these names exist at all. What the Buddhas perceive is that every body is the Dharma-body. One.
All lands are the Buddha-land; all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; all minds are the One Mind.
Even if one searches throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is not the slightest thing—whether form or mind—that is not the principle of the Buddha.

The mirror of wisdom is brilliantly clear, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. There has never been a single thing; the body and mind are tranquil and serene, with nothing to be enacted. This is the Buddha-mind.
Since I am studying Buddha-wisdom and employing the mind as the Buddha does, this is precisely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. When the Buddha manifests, it is my own mind manifesting;
when he does not manifest, it is merely an image upon the mirror of one's own mind. Question: Is it then the case that there are no external Buddhas to be seen at all?

Answer: Self and other are non-dual. However, while the Tathāgata possesses great compassion of identical essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*), sentient beings possess the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) [of delusion].
By the power [of this], one strikes the mirror of the wisdom of the same essence. According to what is perceived on the mind, the images of the marks and signs appear within the mirror;

yet they do not depart from the mirror, nor are they identical to the mirror. Depending on whether what is reflected is beautiful or ugly, the responses vary in a thousand ways and the manifestations differ in ten thousand kinds.
If the capacity (*mārga*) is profound and mature, one may perceive the Buddha’s body as being thousands of millions of *yojanas* in height, with a lifespan of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
In Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within river-sands, he manifests pure and wondrous lands, preaching immeasurable, boundless, ineffable, and unspeakable Dharma-gates.
Whether for those with the distinct retributions of humans and devas, he displays the eight phases of manifestation;

such benefits last no more than several hundred years. Or, for the minute forms of beings with blood in the three miserable realms, they may briefly perceive or hear him through his transformed bodies.
Saving from suffering is like clouds in the sky or the moon in water—vague and indeterminate. All of this arises from the single thought-moment of the one who is moved.
One says that the Buddha’s physical body comes to respond; yet the Buddha is truly without the toil of coming or going, without the affliction of form, and without any dharma that can be spoken.
It is merely that through the wholesome conditions and mental conceptions of sentient beings, they say the Buddha comes to respond and preach the Dharma for them. In reality, it is thus.

Sentient beings merely perceive these images as they appear upon their own minds. Question: Sentient beings’ roots of goodness strike the great, perfect mirror of the Buddha’s wisdom, causing these reflections to appear;
thus, the images would belong to the Buddha. Answer: The clear mirror belongs to the Buddha, but the images do not belong to the Buddha.

If the images belonged to the Buddha, the Buddha would be subject to arising and ceasing, and to flux. If they belonged to sentient beings, then since sentient beings are bound by the fetters of karma, how could [the images] possibly...?
He is endowed with these marks and embellishments; however, it is only when the resonance between sentient beings and the Way intersects that they perceive them. Question:

Since these are images upon the mirror of the Buddha’s wisdom, why is it said that they appear upon the minds of sentient beings? Answer: The perfect mirror of the same essence does not belong exclusively to the Buddha.

Because sentient beings share this same single essence, it is simply that sentient beings have not yet polished their own mirrors to full clarity; therefore, [the image] can only manifest for a brief moment.

This characteristic represents the power of progressive cultivation. Question: If that is so, since sentient beings themselves evoke the manifestation of images upon the mirror of their own minds, one cannot say that Buddha-images appear [by the Buddha's power].
Thus, the Buddha would have no power over sentient beings; what benefit is there in paying empty homage and admiration?
Answer: It is through the power of a heart of reverent admiration that the image appears. This is truly the power of the Buddha; how could it be brought about by sentient beings? Question:

In this case as well, sentient beings receive the Buddha’s power for themselves; it is not the power of another Buddha. Answer: In the stage of Buddhahood, there is no distinction between self and other.
You insist on speaking of self and other; yet the Buddha is nothing other than the inexhaustible mind of sentient beings. Question:

If that is so, then one might as well all together form a single Great Buddha, rather than each individual attaining Buddhahood for themselves. Answer: It is not that they form one together, nor is it that each attains Buddhahood individually.

This principle is difficult to comprehend; let me offer a metaphor by way of introduction. Take, for example, Guoqing Temple: it is the *dharmadhātu*. The monks residing in the temple are the ancient Buddhas.
A traveler from afar visited for a brief time and was moved by the Buddha. On another day, out of deep devotion, he shaved his head and was assigned to Guoqing Temple—which is my temple.

The five peaks, the pine-lined paths, the terraces, halls, chambers, and corridors are all mine; I have suddenly come to enjoy them without diminishing the property of others, and they have become my home.
It is not that each person must build a separate temple, nor is it that one shares a portion with another.
As for the temple, its portions may indeed be taken away by individuals, yet the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena) that abides therein cannot be divided.

This principle is derived from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Along the road there was a great tree; its shade was cool and refreshing, providing shelter to all who came. No one guarded it, and no one took anything away from it.
Since this has been sealed by the golden mouth [of the Buddha], it may be upheld and maintained. Returning and turning back the four lines of verse, one does not perceive the cessation of craving.
"Desire and greed arise. The commentary states that the character "sheng" (arise) is superfluous. Master Daosui said it is not superfluous. "Huanzhuan" (returning and turning) means to overturn;
one does not see [the arising] within the four propositions. "Before desire and greed have ceased" and "desire and greed arise," etc.—the former statement is provisional.

"Dang" (when/at) is a term indicating that [the matter] has not yet been definitively determined. The present statement, "one does not see," is a definitive assertion. Therefore, the two instances are distinct. If one follows this explanation, however...

There are two sets of four phrases; there are no other phrases. According to the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), it proceeds to the second phrase, "non-arising," and thus the character "arising" (*sheng*) is superfluous.

A close examination of the text shows this is inconsistent; it is an erroneous inclusion intended to convey a specific meaning. There is no contradiction with the *Fuxing*, for if attachments are not yet exhausted, they must all be refuted through investigation.
Question: Regarding the sevenfold Two Truths in the *Xuanyan* (Profound Meaning) and the three stages of *zhiguan* (calm abiding and insight), why is there only a fivefold [structure] here?
Answer: Regarding the sequential depth of the arising of the principles of the Truths (*satya*), there are seven meanings; regarding the wisdom of persons, there are only five. Why?

Those who have attained the eighth stage or beyond of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*) and cultivate contemplation upon hearing the Middle Way to suppress their afflictions are called Bodhisattvas; those who shatter ignorance are called Buddhas. The Buddha is the fruit of the Shared Teaching, yet at the level of the fruit there is no person;

this is simply the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhinnayāna*). Therefore, it is called "the Distinct Teaching connecting with the Shared. This applies to both the Distinct and the Perfect Teachings (*vaipulya-yāna*).

Because the two individuals first heard of the Middle Way, it is not called "receiving" (*jiejie*); therefore, there is only one instance of receiving. Question: Since the distinct ground (*bieli*) is identical to the perfect dwelling (*yuanzhu*), why is it not called the perfect receiving?
Answer: Initially, one uses the teaching to receive [the truth], relying on emptiness and the provisional as skillful means (*upāya*).

Only upon realization is it termed a "ground" (*di*). Since the dwelling of the ground is already one, it is no longer called "receiving. Question: Regarding the three instances of receiving mentioned in the *Xuanyiwen*, what do they refer to? Answer: They refer to the receiving of the distinct [vehicle] by the perfect.

As stated in the text: "The Perfect [Teaching] connects with the Shared" means entering the non-successive Three Truths from the Two Truths. "The Perfect connects with the Distinct" means entering the non-successive from the successive.
There are only these three meanings; there are not three distinct types of persons. This is because those of the Distinct Teaching already know the non-successive for themselves.
Thus, there are three in terms of the Truths, but only one in terms of the person. If one were to discuss the fruits of the three teachings according to their actual reality...
There is no one at the head [of the lineage]. One merely cultivates the causes of the Three Teachings to enter the single, perfect fruit (*ekābhisambodhi-phala*).

What need is there for "reception" (*pratigraha*)? What is now called "reception" is merely a conceptual category (*artha-mukha*). Question: "Reception" has the meaning of "connection. Does it mean receiving [the fruit] or entering [the fruit]? Answer:

Between two realms, one must establish a "reception," which resembles the meaning of connection. However, when discussed in terms of ultimate reality, it is simply the act of being received into a distinct state. Within the teachings...
"Not sequential. Question: "What prevents the meaning of 'sequential'? Answer: The text states: "It can only be joined separately; it cannot be joined to what is separate.

If this were the meaning of 'sequential,' then the Separate Teaching would be joined. But how does joining the Separate differ? The text states: "Because this fruit is not used to join the cause of the Ten Grounds, it does not join the Separate.
Because ignorance is severed, it does not join the Ten Abidings. Because it is not [the ultimate], it does not join the Perfect. Question: "The meaning of joining the Separate is as follows..."

The Great Master’s intention was that the four—Sudden, Gradual, Indeterminate, and Secret—constitute the framework of the pedagogical method (*huayi*), encompassing all the temporal teachings of a single lifetime.

The four—Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—constitute the framework of the Dharma (*fafa*), likewise encompassing all the teachings of a single lifetime. If categorized according to the Dharma, the *Lotus Sūtra* is exclusively Perfect (*yuan*).
*Sudden* (*dun*): Among all teachings and all principles, it stands alone without peer or equal. As the text says: "This is the Middle Way that abandons the three provisional means.

If categorized according to the ritual of conversion, it corresponds to the fifth period of gradual teaching. The Great Master stated: "Only the *Avataṃsaka* is sudden; all others belong to the gradual. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says:
"The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* are neither gradual nor sudden. [Regarding] the dust of form and the dust of emptiness...
All possess the merits of a Buddha. There is a great scripture whose essence is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This Dharma-realm resides within the minds of sentient beings;
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the nature of mind are non-dual and indistinguishable. When the mind arises, phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, phenomena cease.

While the nature of the mind is without arising or ceasing, it is able to universally manifest arising and ceasing. Outside of a single thought-moment of mind, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a phenomenon.
It can be attained. This entire mind-nature is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. If for a single thought there is existence, the *dharmadhātu* exists all at once;

if for a single thought there is emptiness, the *dharmadhātu* is empty all at once. When seeing a single speck of dust, one sees the entirety of the *dharmadhātu*. Whether principle or phenomena, the myriad virtues are all perfectly complete.
It is variously named Buddha-nature, Buddha-wisdom, Buddha-virtues, supernormal powers, majestic deportment, or the volumes of the scriptures. Various [names].
Though names differ, their essence does not change; it is neither new nor old, without gain and without loss.
At no time and in no place do they fail to manifest within this single thought-moment of today, clearly and distinctly. This is called the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
All dharmas tend toward desire; there is no way beyond this tendency. Without destroying the body, one accords with the single mark. Lust is itself the Way; hatred... [is itself the Way].
Ignorance (*moha*) is likewise so; there is no decrease in *Aṅgulimāla*. Cultivating the blowing [of breath], one immediately spits [out defilements].

Entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) upon a single speck of dust, one arises from all *samādhis*. All such categories as these are fully contained within this single meaning, as explained in the Ocean of Meanings (*Arthasāgara*).
Copied at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou on the tenth day of the second month in the ninth year of the Dazhong era.
Recorded by the Japanese Tendai monk [Name] Wang, who inquires into the Dharma.
The *Yihai* (Ocean of Meaning) was composed by the Venerable Fazang. His secular surname was Kang; he was originally from the Hu region.

He received the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from Yuan, who in turn had received it from Dushun. The Chan Master’s surname was Du; he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī, as is fully detailed in his biographical records.
Completed on the eighteenth day of the third month in the sixth year of Eiren (1298).
Recorded by the śramaṇa Zen’e.
